clue.text: Too inept to move like a ballet dancer, perhaps

indicators.note: letters made to move around are being rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is too clumsy ever to dance like a ballerina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to move' is the anagram signal on TOO INEPT; 'perhaps' marks the ballet dancer as only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballet dancers in pointe work balance up on the tips of their toes.

clue.text: Amount to part of a whole account

parts.note: to amount to something is to be it
a half is one part of a whole

explanation.surface: A bookkeeper describes a sum forming a share of a bigger total account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Account' looks like bookkeeping but is the definition, as in 'on my account'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'On behalf of' and 'on account of' both mean for the sake of someone or something.

clue.text: Says with stammering tongue, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means taking the opening letter of each of the two words before it

parts.note: to say is to utter

explanation.surface: A description of someone speaking haltingly, catching on the first sounds.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters of 'stammering' and 'tongue' go in front of UTTERS; the whole clue also defines it, a stammerer repeating word beginnings.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stutters speaks with a stammer, repeating initial sounds.

clue.text: Money maintains company known for flying fortress in Africa

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so the money word holds the other piece within it

parts.note: cash is money
BA is British Airways, an airline

explanation.surface: Cash keeps an airline in business.
explanation.definitionFit: A casbah is the citadel of a North African city, as in Algiers.

clue.text: Foreign nobleman and ruler on horse

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece on another means it follows it

parts.note: horse and junk are both slang for heroin
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: A foreign aristocrat and a monarch ride a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horse' is not the animal but drug slang for heroin, like junk.
explanation.definitionFit: A Junker was a member of the Prussian landed aristocracy.

clue.text: Judge present Times journalist to be doomed

parts.note: present means in, as in at home
X is the multiplication sign, read as times
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A judge decides a journalist at The Times is finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the newspaper but is the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: Jinxed means under a curse, hence bound for bad luck.

clue.text: Attack right back stops posing no threat

indicators.note: a stopper sits in a gap, so this piece goes inside the other

parts.note: safe means posing no threat

indicators.note: back means the right abbreviation is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A footballer's right back halts an attack that was harmless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right back' is a football position on the surface; here 'back' turns RT round.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with gunfire from low-flying aircraft.

clue.text: Code cracked by unspecified number of people in a group

indicators.note: something cracked open has another piece let into it

parts.note: an ethic is a code of moral conduct
N stands for an unspecified number in maths

explanation.surface: A cipher is broken by an unknown number of people working together.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethnic describes things relating to a group of people sharing culture or descent.

clue.text: One on board managing rough treatment

parts.note: a chess or draughts piece on the board is a man
managing means handling

explanation.surface: A company director handling things gets treated roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on board' suggests a company board; the man is a piece on a games board.
explanation.definitionFit: Manhandling means pushing or dragging someone about with physical force.

clue.text: Left-wing militants rejected a suit jacket from Norma

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the whole string is read in reverse

parts.note: to suit is to fit

indicators.note: the jacket of a word is its outer covering, the first and last letters

explanation.surface: Radicals turn down a suit jacket that Norma offers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' reverses A, FIT and NA (the jacket, or outside letters, of Norma) together.
explanation.definitionFit: Antifa is a loose movement of anti-fascist activists, often militant.

clue.text: Where cars race about madly, dashing at intervals

indicators.note: letters behaving madly are thrown into a new order
taking letters at intervals means every other one from dashing

explanation.surface: Cars rush about wildly, speeding along at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges ABOUT; 'at intervals' takes A, H, N from 'dashing'.
explanation.definitionFit: German motorways, famous for stretches with no speed limit, are fast roads.

clue.text: Ironstone in social gathering

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British weight

explanation.surface: Ironstone lies within a party gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's single word 'Ironstone' splits into Iron and stone; a stone is a British weight of 14 pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A fest is a festival or celebratory gathering.

clue.text: Overture from Fauré playing, then I hear scale

indicators.note: an overture is an opening, so this takes the first letter of the composer's name
letters playing about are being rearranged

explanation.surface: An overture by Fauré is performed, then I hear a musical scale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scale' looks musical but is a temperature scale; 'playing' rearranges THEN I HEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The Fahrenheit temperature scale puts freezing water at 32 degrees.

clue.text: Eager man is in Guardian presses producing a Berliner version?

indicators.note: the words press around the answer, holding it inside them

explanation.surface: A keen man at the Guardian's presses turns out a Berliner-format paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian once printed in the Berliner format; the answer sits inside the words, running into the G of Guardian.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something Berliner, German in style, is to Germanise it.

clue.text: Patron Saint oppressed by a menace abroad

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece oppressed by another sits underneath it
abroad means all over the place, so these letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A holy patron is weighed down by a threat from overseas.
explanation.definitionFit: Maecenas was the Roman backer of Virgil and Horace, his name now meaning a generous sponsor of the arts.

clue.text: Most wanting to stop working in tense shifts

indicators.note: the stopping piece goes in the rearranged letters
the letters shift about into a new order

parts.note: a machine that stops working dies

explanation.surface: Workers in tense shifts are desperate to stop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifts' looks like work rotas but is the anagram signal, and 'in' puts the stopping word inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The neediest are those in the greatest want or poverty.

clue.text: Dangerous creatures in lingerie business, at first

indicators.note: at first means this short piece comes before the other

parts.note: Co is short for company, a business
bras are lingerie

explanation.surface: Something dangerous lurks in an underwear firm's early days.
explanation.definitionFit: Cobras are venomous snakes, so a threat to anyone nearby.

clue.text: Repeatedly say nothing about heartless executive? How exasperating!

indicators.note: the doubled hush goes about, around, the other piece
repeatedly means the call for silence is given twice over

parts.note: sh is a call to say nothing

indicators.note: heartless means the whole middle of executive is cut out, leaving its two ends

explanation.surface: Someone keeps quiet about a callous boss, and gets exasperated.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheesh is an interjection of irritation or disbelief.

clue.text: Breed of pet rat eating pork pie wife brought around

indicators.note: the outer word eats, takes in, the other piece

parts.note: a rat or rotter is a scoundrel

indicators.note: brought around means turned to face the other way, read backwards

parts.note: pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for lie

explanation.surface: A dog eats a pork pie the owner's wife brought round.
explanation.walkthrough: Pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang, a London habit; 'brought around' turns the lie and W into WEIL, which 'eating' puts inside the rat.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rottweiler is a German dog breed kept as guard dog or companion.

clue.text: Brown coats unusual for top Democrat

indicators.note: the colour word coats, covers, the other piece

parts.note: tan is a brown colour
rum means odd or unusual in British slang

explanation.surface: Brown paint covers something strange belonging to a party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brown' suggests the British politician Gordon Brown, but is just the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Truman was a Democrat who reached the top job, US president.

clue.text: Remind people of lecherous fellow getting ahead

parts.note: a rake is a dissolute, lecherous man
up means ahead, as in being up in a game

explanation.surface: A womaniser gets on in life and people remember.
explanation.definitionFit: To rake up an old matter is to revive something best forgotten.

clue.text: Genuine article returned broken by Charlie

indicators.note: broken by means the other piece splits this one open
returned means read backwards

parts.note: the is the definite article
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A genuine object comes back damaged by Charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: Echt is a German loanword meaning authentic or real.

clue.text: Miss one buried in funeral ground

indicators.note: a buried piece is put inside the other
ground means crushed and broken up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone is lost and laid in the burial ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'funeral ground' reads as graveyard, but 'ground' rearranges FUNERAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Fräulein is the German title for an unmarried woman, like Miss.

clue.text: Half-heartedly mouth entertaining answer for emperor

indicators.note: to entertain is to take in, so the shortened word holds the other letter
half the heart is lost: one of the two middle letters is dropped

parts.note: kisser is slang for mouth

explanation.surface: Someone mumbles a reply to an emperor without conviction.
explanation.walkthrough: KISSER has a double S at its heart; 'Half-heartedly' drops one, leaving KISER to take in A.
explanation.definitionFit: Kaiser was the title of the German emperors, from Latin Caesar.

clue.text: Left-leaning parties saving time where men were detained

indicators.note: saving means keeping inside, holding the other letter
in an across answer, leaning left means reading right to left, backwards

parts.note: galas are parties

explanation.surface: Socialist parties claw back time from the place where men are held.
explanation.definitionFit: A Stalag was a German prisoner-of-war camp in the Second World War.

clue.text: Regime change in places with extremes of temperature

parts.note: to place something is to put it
C and H stand for cold and hot, the two extremes, as on taps

explanation.surface: Climate change hits places with very hot and cold weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremes' looks like first and last letters of temperature, but means cold and hot.
explanation.definitionFit: A putsch is a sudden attempt to overthrow a government by force, a coup.
